items.item: The half-open range convention [lo, hi): lo is always a candidate, hi is always one past the last candidate
A loop invariant for binary search must be stated and kept true at the top of every iteration, not just argued informally
lower_bound: first index i with a[i] >= x
upper_bound: first index i with a[i] > x (or the end of the range if none)
First and last occurrence of x reduce to lower_bound(x) and upper_bound(x) - 1
The count of x in a sorted range equals upper_bound(x) - lower_bound(x)
The naive midpoint (low + high) / 2 overflows a fixed-width signed integer for large enough low and high

at.step: The bug that waited nine years

items.item: The portable, overflow-safe midpoint is low + ((high - low) / 2)

items.item: The same bug sat undetected in Bentley's Programming Pearls binary search and in the JDK's own Arrays.binarySearch for about nine years before it was reported

at.step: The bug that waited nine years

items.item: The bug manifests only at array lengths around 2^30 (roughly a billion elements), which is why it went unnoticed for two decades

at.step: The bug that waited nine years

items.item: Java's own shipped fix uses an unsigned right shift (low + high) >>> 1, a language-specific alternative to the portable form
Termination: each iteration strictly shrinks hi - lo (by at least one), so the loop ends in at most ceil(lg(n+1)) iterations for an array of n elements
The exact number of iterations for n = 1,000,000 is 20
A closed-range [lo, hi] formulation of the same algorithm needs a different, easier-to-break empty-range and termination check, which is why this topic standardises on half-open
Binary search needs random access to the range (an array, not a linked list), a precondition named but not explored here
